aliases.name: Nurarihyon
aliases.meaning: From 'nurari' (to slip away) + 'hyon' (onomatopoeia for floating upward); written 滑瓢 ('slippery gourd')

aliases.name: Sea-monster nurarihyon
aliases.meaning: Globe-shaped umibōzu-like creature in the Seto Inland Sea

description.summary: An Edo-period Japanese yōkai depicted as an old man with an elongated, gourd-shaped head, originally an obscure figure in yōkai picture scrolls, later popularised in twentieth-century media as a refined intruder and supreme commander of yōkai.
description.full: Nurarihyon (滑瓢, ぬらりひょん) is a Japanese yōkai whose first surviving images come from Edo-period yōkai picture scrolls (yōkai emaki), notably Sawaki Suushi's Hyakkai Zukan (1737) and Toriyama Sekien's Gazu Hyakki Yagyō. Early images show a wizened, bald, gourd-headed old man in fine kimono or Buddhist robes, often associated with a kago (palanquin), but no narrative is attached. Its now-famous behaviour — slipping into a busy household at dusk, seating himself, drinking the family's tea and being accepted as the master of the house through sheer composure — derives from a 1929 caption written by folklorist Morihiko Fujisawa under Sekien's image, identifying him as 'the chief of the yōkai who comes to visit'. Folklorists Kenji Murakami and Katsumi Tada have noted that this is a modern interpretive reading rather than a documented folktale. In Okayama Prefecture, nurarihyon appears as a different creature: a spherical floating yōkai in the Seto Inland Sea, akin to the umibōzu, that bobs out of fishermen's reach. Twentieth-century manga (notably Mizuki Shigeru's GeGeGe no Kitarō from the 1960s onward) elevated nurarihyon to 'supreme commander of all yōkai' (yōkai no sōtaishō), a status without basis in the Edo sources but now central to its popular identity, reinforced by works such as Hiroshi Shiibashi's Nura: Rise of the Yokai Clan and the antagonist of the same name in Demon Slayer (Kimetsu no Yaiba).

etymology.origin: Japanese; from nurari (滑り, 'slipping, slithering') + hyon (瓢, the character for gourd, also an onomatopoeia of something popping or floating up)
etymology.meaning: Approximately 'the slippery gourd' or 'the slipping-away one', alluding both to the elongated gourd-shaped head and to the creature's elusive nature
etymology.first_use: Documented in Edo-period yōkai picture scrolls; the Bakemono no e attributed to Kanō Motonobu's lineage (c. 1700) and Sawaki Suushi's Hyakkai Zukan (1737)

related_phenomena.name: Umibōzu

features.description: Bald, swollen, often described as cucurbit- or eggplant-shaped; the most distinctive trait
Wizened, wrinkled face; sometimes likened to a cross between an old man and a catfish
Wears elegant kimono or Buddhist abbot's kasaya, suggesting wealth or rank
Edo-period scrolls depict nurarihyon stepping out of, or hanging from, a black palanquin

physical.morphology: Humanoid with disproportionately large, elongated, gourd-shaped cranium. In the Okayama variant, an entirely different morphology: a globe-shaped floating creature in the sea.

abilities.description: Modern characterisation: slips into a home unnoticed and is accepted as its master through unflappable bearing
Twentieth-century media depict nurarihyon as the 'supreme commander' or general of the yōkai (yōkai no sōtaishō)
Etymologically 'the slippery one'; in Okayama tradition the floating sphere sinks just as fishermen reach it

behavior.diet: Tea and household refreshments (in modern characterisation)
patterns: Arrives during the busy evening meal hour
Behaves with the calm authority of the head of household
Cannot easily be expelled because residents take him for the master

range.description: A pan-Japanese folklore figure; specific regional traditions in Akita Prefecture (as a member of the night parade) and Okayama Prefecture (sea-creature variant). Modern media-driven popularity is national.
regions: Edo (modern Tokyo) — origin of the principal scrolls

hotspots.name: Seto Inland Sea (Okayama variant)
hotspots.notes: Local fishermen's tradition of a floating, head-sized sphere identified as nurarihyon

hotspots.name: Sae no Kamizaka

location.description: Sae no Kamizaka pass, modern Yuzawa, Akita Prefecture

hotspots.notes: Ethnographer Sugae Masumi's 1814 travel record places nurarihyon in a hyakki yagyō there

first_recorded.source: Bakemono no e attributed to the Kanō Motonobu lineage; firmly attested in Sawaki Suushi's Hyakkai Zukan (1737)

peak_activity_periods.description: Iconographic establishment in yōkai picture scrolls
Reinterpretation as 'master of the house' beginning with Morihiko Fujisawa's 1929 captions
Mass-media role as supreme commander of yōkai through Mizuki Shigeru's GeGeGe no Kitarō and successors

origins.cultural_roots: Edo-period yōkai picture scrolls (yōkai emaki) by professional painters of the Kanō and Tosa schools and by yōkai specialists such as Toriyama Sekien.
origins.earliest_accounts: No surviving folktale predates the Edo-period images; nurarihyon enters the record as an iconographic figure rather than as the protagonist of an oral tale.
origins.folklore_connections: Linked iconographically to the Hyakki Yagyō (Night Parade of a Hundred Demons) tradition; in Okayama, conceptually linked to umibōzu sea spirits.

timeline.event: Image of nurarihyon appears in the Bakemono no e attributed to the Kanō Motonobu lineage
Sawaki Suushi includes nurarihyon in Hyakkai Zukan
Toriyama Sekien depicts nurarihyon in Gazu Hyakki Yagyō
timeline.significance: Popularises the figure among Edo readers

timeline.event: Sugae Masumi records nurarihyon as a participant in a hyakki yagyō at Sae no Kamizaka, Akita
timeline.significance: Earliest known textual placement in regional folklore

timeline.event: Morihiko Fujisawa publishes captions identifying nurarihyon as 'the chief monster who comes to visit'
timeline.significance: Origin of the 'master of the house' interpretation

timeline.event: Mizuki Shigeru begins serialising GeGeGe no Kitarō, reusing nurarihyon as a recurring character
timeline.significance: Foundation of the modern pop-culture image

timeline.event: Hiroshi Shiibashi launches Nura: Rise of the Yokai Clan in Weekly Shōnen Jump, with nurarihyon as central protagonist's lineage
timeline.significance: Cements the 'commander of yōkai' archetype globally

history.modern_era: Nurarihyon is now one of the most internationally recognised yōkai, largely through manga, anime and video games. Folklorists distinguish the historically thin Edo iconography from the rich modern characterisation; debates continue over whether modern reinterpretation enriches or distorts the tradition (Natsuhiko Kyōgoku and Kunihiro Shimura take opposing positions).

documentary.name: Hyakkai Zukan
documentary.description: Illustrated handscroll by Sawaki Suushi depicting nurarihyon among other yōkai; one of the earliest dated surviving images.
documentary.analysis: Foundational iconographic source for the gourd-headed humanoid form.

documentary.name: Gazu Hyakki Yagyō
documentary.description: Toriyama Sekien's printed compendium of yōkai including nurarihyon.
documentary.analysis: Mass-printed; primary route by which the image entered popular culture.

paranormal.name: Yōkai with origins in floating sea creatures
paranormal.description: In the Okayama tradition, nurarihyon are physical sea creatures that, having gathered influence, migrate to land and become household-haunting yōkai; a transition motif also seen with umibōzu.
evidence_cited: Seto Inland Sea sightings of head-sized floating spheres

scientific.name: Misidentified marine fauna (Okayama variant)
scientific.description: Observed 'floating heads' in the Seto Inland Sea may correspond to large jellyfish (e.g. Nemopilema nomurai), Portuguese man o' war, or partly submerged squid.
proponents: Modern Japanese folklorists, summarised in Wikipedia
evidence_cited: Known abundance of large jellyfish in the Seto Inland Sea

skeptical.name: Modern invention through caption-folklore
skeptical.description: The 'master of the house' character is a 20th-century literary invention by Morihiko Fujisawa (1929), retroactively applied to an originally narrativeless image.
evidence_cited: Direct textual analysis of Fujisawa's captions

stories: Nurarihyon as a polite intruder into a home at dusk (modern, post-Fujisawa)
Nurarihyon as a head-sized sphere in the Seto Inland Sea (Okayama)
folklore.beliefs: Treated as a curio of yōkai literature rather than a feared spirit; modern audiences encounter it primarily through media.

literature: Nura: Rise of the Yokai Clan — Hiroshi Shiibashi (2008–2012)
